source.drive: AMAF 2026 3(  Transition to breakouts  &  Midwifery Models of Care in the African Continent  & Day 1 Wrap-Up & Synthesis)

segments.text: I hope everyone's feeling refreshed after lunch. So I moderated the last session and I made sure we left one o'clock on the dot for lunch. So let's also do this one also as per the time.

So this next session fits very well with what we've just been, we had a session before lunch. Because before lunch, we talked about what is it that we need from the midwives? What is their role? How can they support? And it also talked about then how can we prepare them? How can they be trained, supported, supervised, mentored? Which was great and we got out of perspectives. Now if we have them deployed, how can we retain them? How can we ensure they have safe and supportive and accountable workplaces? How can we use data to discuss and work on some of these? So for this session, we're going to have it in kind of two ways.

We'll have two presenters and then two panelists. And the presenters are going to give us great introductory presentations because there'll be a presentation on research findings, on strategic models for deployment, workforce optimization and retention. And we're also going to have a very, another interesting presentation on, we talk about how midwives are the frontline workers.

We talk about the importance of midwives in the prevention of preventable maternal deaths. So we're also going to hear some research findings or studies on what is really driving maternal and child health within 55 AU member states. So let's look at what are the drivers, what are the causes? We link to those who are supposed to help us prevent these causes to happen.

So we'll look at this evidence on some of the strategies for deployment, optimization and retention. We'll look at what is driving these deaths, preventable deaths. We're also going to hear now experiences from two countries.

How are they actually dealing with this? How are they working on deployment retention? And this is from context which is of humanitarian but also development. So this will fit in into what the data is saying, what are some of the strategies for what's actually happening on the ground. So for this, we have four great presenters.
I'd like to welcome them in front. We have Professor Doreen Kaura from University of Western Cape. Please clap and have a seat here.
And then we have Eba Sako from Africa CDC. Please come have a seat. And we'll also have a chance to hear from the countries, from Burkina Faso and from Nigeria.

So I will invite them once the presenters have made their presentation to come here to join the panel. So without further ado, I'd welcome, yes, you can come and present from here, and we take it from there. We do our best to keep to ten minutes to allow for the discussions.
And again, the two presentations will be in English, so have your headphones. But when it comes to the panelists, it will be English and French. Welcome.
Good afternoon. It's me again. I know we are quite full, which is nice.
But please don't sleep. Thank you. I think this afternoon, we are reflecting on midwife-led units and a strategic model of deployment, workforce optimization, and retention.

I think when we speak about midwifery models of care, they've been in Africa for a very long time. We have been working with them since 1984 in South Africa, in Kenya, in Senegal, and other spaces. So for once, I think that the North will learn from the South how we operate the midwifery models of care.

I'm going to present a splint analysis, because when the WHO introduced the midwifery models of care, the Gates Foundation came together, and they wanted to look at what kind of models of care do we have in Africa. So we looked at two countries, which is Senegal and Kenya, in order to inform evidence and raise awareness on these midwifery models of care. So that was the main objective, and to understand the midwifery models of care, the innovations that are there, how do we have high-impact innovations within a context of low-middle-income countries.

The research explored what defines a strong, successful midwifery program within the context of Africa, and what are the constraints that the midwives are facing, that they are not being able to develop these models further. So in Kenya, the research was led by the Africa Institute for Development and Policy, AFIDEP, and in Senegal, it was led by the Institute for Research and Epidemiological Surveillance. So the study used a mixed-methods research approach.

We had these two multiple case studies. We started with a literature review of frameworks of guidelines that inform midwifery models of care, and then we did a stakeholder mapping in each of the countries and technical working groups that are involved within the midwifery models of care. We also had county and region selections, and also the health facility selection.
I was not part of the research group, but we were the advisors. We had three advisors during the project. I was one of them, and the project was led by Dr. Jennifer.

So the data collection methods were in-depth interviews, key informant interviews, and also health facility observations, and we did a secondary analysis of the literature review. We also did a synthesis and final report. Not moving.
There we go. Now, this conceptual framework is what came about from the study. If you look at it, it's showing the midwifery models of care conceptual framework as the output of the work.

The inner ring is the macroenvironment. I mean, the outer ring is the macroenvironment within which these midwifery models of care operate, which are influenced by the governance, the policy, the financing, which we were talking about this morning that also influences education. The meso and macroenvironment was influenced by human resources, infrastructure, commodities, and referrals, and most of these facilities were not well-resourced.

So when we speak about the inner core, we wanted to see what do we mean by high performance within these midwifery models of care. And on the right were the outcomes that we were looking for and the impact that we were looking for. So just a brief, because I'm going to run through this because I have only 10 minutes, just a brief of the Senegal findings is that between 2017 and 2023, Senegal had a 35% reduction of maternal mortality rates from 236 to 153, which was great.

This shows that, and most of the causes of maternal mortality in this incidence was obstetric hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders. We also had postpartum hemorrhage, and also within 24 hours of admission, some of them were unknown causes. But in that essence, we also realized that we can't blame the structure of the space.

I'm forgetting to turn this thing. So the midwifery-led care models, there were five different models within Senegal. We had that which was midwife-led at health centers, where the midwife was the lead in those health centers.

We also had the collaborative physician-midwife care, where the physician was also involved in the low-risk and high-risk care, but mostly in hospitals. And then we had midwife-led care at health posts, where the midwife was in charge of that care. We also had a midwifery model, which was called SAFI, where midwife-led care across the continuum, that's antenatal, intranatal, postnatal, and neonatal care.

And they provided these facilities within the community also. We had another one that was called the, not to go, if I'm pronouncing it right, accommodation of high-risk pregnancies, where the clients of complications stay in the host families close to the health facilities before delivery, and not necessarily in the hospital. So we can see there are different structures of these models of care within Senegal.

And then when we looked at how midwives-led low-risk care at the health centers, you can see in antenatal, the midwife was the lead. There wasn't even a doctor, but the doctor was available for referral. Delivery care, there was a midwife.

During complications, there was a midwife. Who was the lead? And even postnatal and during the MNCH. So we had the type one and two, which was type one health centers, and type two, which were shared by the obstetricians.

So then we had this other one, where midwifery-led care was autonomous in the health posts, because there were no doctors to consult there mostly. So it was the midwives looking at the whole continuum of care without any doctors in charge in these spaces. And if we compare the Kenyan context, where we had four different models that we looked at, there was the midwifery-led routine care model, there was the midwife-led dedicated maternity unit, there was collaborative shared care model, and there was also community-linked midwifery care model.
Midwives are very important. It is going. So those are the models of care we are talking about.

And then we have them in the level two dispensary, where the midwife-led care model was there, and linked to the community with the community health workers. And then we had the level three health center, which was a collaborative shared care model, linked to midwifery-led routine care model. We had level four and five, which was shared care, where the midwives would consult and refer to the obstetricians or the doctors in level four and five and six.
And that happened throughout the structure. So the next... Sorry, I don't know. Let me go back.

Yeah, so the midwives-led routine care, where they escalated complications, they saw the woman during antenatal, intranatal, during delivery, and there was a transition. Because, remember, delivery is... You require swift responses. So there was a collaborative shared care, where the doctors were alerted that there is a delivery which could possibly be a complication.

And postnatal and RMCH was mostly the midwives-led this type of care. Another one was collaborative care in high-risk areas, where mostly the doctors were the leads, but the midwives were supporting this kind of care. Then when we came to the Kenya Community Health Promoters link between women and the midwifery-led care, Kenya had a very transitional community health promoters, where they were integrated into the system.

For antenatal, they were the primary in the community, where they would identify pregnant women and encourage them to get antenatal services. And then during delivery, they would also support the women to get to the facilities which were needed. And also follow up during postnatal care.

They were also support... They were providing support services in some of the other centres that we looked at. So if we think about the cross-country insight between Kenya and Senegal, midwives lead routine care autonomously across most models of facility care levels. In both countries, we had a shift to collaborative care with doctors and high-risk cases.

Do we need midwives? Do we need midwives? Can we do without midwives? Community-based approaches extend midwifery reach in both countries through mobile outreach. So there is a lot of consultation and there is a lot of collaboration, but the midwife is the centre in most of these communities. The health system factors, which include training, supportive suspension, adequate infrastructure, and commodities, were a challenge in both contexts.

But person-centred care consistently enables midwifery models to perform excellently in both countries. Staff shortages was a problem in both countries. Equipment gaps, variable in-service training, constrained midwifery performance across facilities and regions.

And this was a big frustration for midwives. They want to stay within the midwifery-led units because they feel empowered to be with the woman within this. Those were some of the statements that they said.

But without the resources, they don't want to be there. The outcome is that person-centred and respectful maternity is central to midwife philosophy in both countries, emphasising dignity, autonomy, continuity of care, and midwifery care is associated with improved outcomes. So thank you so much that shared leadership will help us achieve these enablers, which is education, person-centred, and financial.
And this is the model that we developed, which is going to be published soon. So policy investment priorities for midwife models of care is ultimate and it's necessary. And thank you.
Thank you very much. Food for thought. Good results.

It shows us the direction. It shows the role, leadership, the health system changes, but more important, what are the outcomes if we get it right? So now I'd ask my colleague from Africa CDC to also come and make his presentation so we see what is it, which women are we trying to save? Why are they dying? So we see those that we're going to deploy and retain, what are the work ahead of them? So please come and share your perspectives. Thank you very much.

I bring you greetings from the Africa CDC. That's the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And for those that don't know, it's a continental institution that is responsible for protecting Africa health sovereignty and security as far as health is concerned.

And it's my pleasure to bring you greetings from Dr. Diana, who is the head of Division of RAMCA at the Africa CDC. My name is Ibar Seka. I'm a senior technical officer working with the Africa CDC under the Centers for Primary Health Care.
You will agree with me that in recent midwifery practice must be evident-based. So we are advocating for evident-based midwifery practice. And in that, we need to know what are the evidence.

So we must have to do that through using systematic research. Africa CDC conducted a study that covered all the 55 member states. And just at the start, you will agree with me that 70% of the maternal deaths are in Africa.

And in the absolute figures that we had in 2023, when we looked at the study in all the 55 member states, indicated 178,600 women died in 2003. That is definitely very stark. The role of midwives in that is very critical.

So when we go forward and look at the maternal mortality ratio, that's telling us that 388 per 100,000 live birth. And if we project towards the target of the SDGs, which we expect to have 170 per 100,000 live birth, we'll be at 330 per 100,000 live birth. The figures are definitely very stark and are very high.

Understanding the next level, we collected this data, triangulated the collection of this data. One, national death reviews in individual countries were reviewed. You know that countries performed maternal and peridatal death reviews.

Those records were reviewed. And we collected data from those countries. From all the 55 member states, which was analysed, supported by the UN global figures, supported by evidence, literatures that are coming from peer-reviewed journals.

So it means the data process was further, you know, triangulated as a form of validation of getting the facts that are in this, all the 55 African Union members here. Take, for example, 199 documents from 34 member states were reviewed. And all the 55 member states were also involved.

We validated this inviting all the member states sub-regionally in Kenya and in Cotonou to validate the facts involving the member states who are very key in this. So when we did that, further down, interestingly, this is a very interesting slide. Let's look at what is killing the mothers and also what are killing the newborns.

First of all, hemorrhage, you will agree with me, that 72% of the member states claim that hemorrhage is the one sentencing the mothers to death. And further, literatures include that close to 36% of maternal deaths are due to hemorrhage. The role of the midwives in controlling that high blood loss following delivery is definitely very critical.
The skills that the midwife needed in saving the lives of the mother is very critical. Imagine a woman delivers and bleeding heavily. All of a sudden, collapse.

Those skills that you see need, like the condom tamponade. So that's why in Africa CDC, when we did the online pre-event survey, we felt midwives and doctors need to have the skills to save the lives of the mothers. Then we conducted studies, and we followed by trainings on emergency obstetrics and newborn care services.

The models we developed, the curriculums, and we work with more member states in doing that. First, we prioritize 25 African Union member states that recorded the highest maternal mortality. We give them the skills.
The skills are very important. If you look at it further down, you will see in two countries, like in Ethiopia, the direct causes were close to 61%. I'm on the same slide.
61% is a very important slide, sir. The next point is hypertensive disorder. Take, for example, in Uganda.
In 2001, it was 15%. It rose to 21% in 2004. And countries like Lesotho and Malawi, now hypertensive disorders are claiming the highest.
So the role of the midwives comes in here. The skills that we need. I'm on the same slide.
Anemia, HIV. HIV compounded the situation. And the fifth, interestingly, when the reviews were done, some of the causes of the death were not known.
Interesting. And if you come also to the babies, most of them were dying. Three quarters of the deaths were due to intrapartum asphyxia and prematurity.

And you will agree with me that. There comes the part of the management that the use of the corticosteroids and the kangaroo motor care, in which the midwife is also okay. But interestingly, some of these deaths need to be audited.
But some of them were not done. The midwives are key in the auditing process. The audit itself saves the life.
Using further models. That's the magnitude. And I said, it's greatest now in Western Africa.
You can see the deaths. But Nigeria alone, five countries, if you compound them together, we are responsible of 64% of the death. Nigeria alone claimed for 42%.
Perhaps due to extreme values. The population is too big. The time is limited, actually.
The reports are available online on our Africa CDC. You can get it. You can get both reports that are there.
So you can see, it's only nine countries that use the MANIA and the TELIA model to do that. Asset avoidability of death is only nine out of 34. Tracts and work on the recommendation is only nine.
So now, let's look at the three zeros. One continental promise. What is the role of the midwives? Interestingly.

Her Excellency, Dr. Samir Sulu, has said, a political promise, one stronger primary healthcare system, citizens can be understood, leaders can be held accountable. Very interesting. Zero home delivery.
We emphasize zero home delivery. Zero preventable maternal death. And zero unfortunate child.
The role of the midwife is very critical in these three. So I think I didn't have time. I'll stop here.
You can get both reports, the continental reports and the AU Champion Roadmap report on our website, Africa CDC website. I thank you very much. Bonjour à tous.
Okay. Thank you very much. I think the second presentation took us to additional data.

Why are women dying? What are the causes? Preventable. If we have skilled midwives, skilled workforce, we can prevent, we can save these mothers and newborns. But are we getting the midwives deployed where they need to be? Are we retaining them, even in some places which are hard to reach, which are underserved, rural and urban? This is what our two colleagues from Burkina Faso and Nigeria will give us the perspectives of getting the midwives deployed and retained to respond to what we've just heard.

Prepare your headphones because we'll start with Burkina Faso and it will be presented by Madame Maïga Maimouna, who's the president of the National Council of Order of Midwives of Burkina Faso. I'll ask her to just share some perspectives so that we can see what is happening from that perspective or from her perspective in Burkina Faso. I'll ask the question in French, so have your headphones.

Madame Maïmouna, in the humanitarian context, midwives are often the only providers of services for sexual and reproductive health. They have to face physical insecurity, destruction of infrastructure, but also challenges in terms of supply chains. In light of Burkina Faso's experience, what political reforms of financial institutions or support and protection have proven to be the most effective in deploying midwives in high-risk areas, but also in maintaining them? What is Burkina Faso's experience? Hello everyone.

Thank you for this opportunity to communicate. In relation to the political reforms that have proven to be really effective in deploying and maintaining midwives in high-risk areas, there is first of all the massive recruitment of midwives and midwives. 300 midwives are recruited each year in direct contests and 400 in professional contests.

That's a large number, so it really helps to meet personnel needs. In addition to that, there is an organization at Burkina Faso, that is, the organization of a very important that really allows midwives to work safely in high-risk areas. There is the implementation of the minimum emergency device in the USSR, the DMU-SSR.

There is also the sanitary reserve. The sanitary reserve consists of midwives and midwives who have been trained but who have not been recruited by the public service. These midwives are skilled and have quite advanced skills.

They are trained, they are there, and technical and financial partners such as the UNFPA and MSF recruit these midwives to strengthen their skills and they are affected in difficult areas. There is also the organization of services that ensures that when a team is on the ground, it is during a delay and then we relay them and get them out and bring in a new team. There is also the fact that the government has obtained a specific geographical indemnity for all health personnel who really work in difficult areas.

There is also the establishment of an integrated center for violence based on people that we call the One Stop Center. It is an integrated center for violence. There is also the psychological care of the midwives, of all the personnel who work in these difficult areas.

In addition to all these actions, there is the field visit of the largest health authorities. We have shown that the minister often travels with humanitarian flights and goes to difficult areas to encourage the staff. In addition to that, there are congratulations, honorary distinctions that are given to the midwives to really encourage them.

Not to mention the reinforcement of capacities, first locally, in the form of tutoring, training by mentors, mentors who are on the ground. There are also facilities that are given to these midwives who work in difficult areas. When the humanitarian flights are available, they are prioritized to visit their families and then come back.

In terms of success, these are actions that have shown that we have managed to have a continuity of care despite this difficult situation. There has been an improvement in reproductive sexual health in all the regions of Burkina Faso and an improvement in the number of visits. We have also managed to create a professional environment that is favorable to the birth of midwives.
Thank you. Thank you very much. Just as we looked at the models of care, we looked at the data where women are dying, you can imagine in a situation of humanitarian crisis, this is even greater.

The experience shared from Burkina Faso is some effort that are done. I think what's important, there are some very high-level policy decisions to make this happen, but there are also some specifics that also went to support the midwives themselves in terms of allowances, in terms of even their security. Let's not forget that in these insecure areas, even the midwives are insecure.

They also need protection, not only to serve, but they also need to be protected. This is an example of what happens on the ground to respond to the data and evidence we saw. Now we'll ask some experience from Nigeria.

We have our colleague who is the CEO of the Nurse and Midwifery Council of Nigeria. What we want to learn from you is Nigeria has significantly expanded nursing and midwifery enrollment to close the critical workforce gaps. But we know that producing more midwives does not automatically mean they'll be retained in the rural areas.

From a regulatory standpoint, how are you aligning this? The pre-service curricula, competency standards, exposure to the rural settings, and actually motivating them to practice in the rural settings. How are you managing this in Nigeria? Thank you very much. I'm happy to be here.

I listened attentively to the presentation of the two presenters, but most interestingly, the one presented by the CDC officer, which shows how bad it is in Nigeria. However, let me start by saying that like you did say in your introduction, population-wise, Nigeria is a large population. Presently, Nigeria is estimated to be over 250 million people.

Covering the communities is a bit of a challenge, but not a challenge because the government saw this coming far back in 2003. In 2003, Nigeria had winded up the training of basic midwives, but the figure as it was coming up that time, alerted the government to say, something is happening at the maternity section. Do something.

To that, the government of the Federation directed the Northern and Middle Free Council of Nigeria to reestablish basic midwifery training as an intervention program that would last for 10 years. After 10 years, we reported back to the government that the intervention program earlier planned as studies bound, but the government said, no, the problem is still not solved. Continue.

To that extent, they noticed that even the basic midwives they asked us to train, when they finish training, they don't want to go to the remote areas where these maternity deaths are happening, so that we should come up with another program that will make sure that the communities are well covered. Prior to then, in 1987, when the primary healthcare concept was to be introduced, the doctors said they are not going to the rural areas, the nurses, the midwives said they are not going to the rural areas, so the government of the then administration introduced what was known as community health extension workers. They are the primary people managing the primary healthcare centers.

Then, the question is, are they delivering? If they've been delivering to expectation, why should we still be having this ego? That was what prompted the government to say that, okay, these people are not competent enough to solve the problem. 2012, Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria was asked to reintroduce community nursing and community midwifery programs. When it was to be introduced, it was not made composable for all the states, for all the schools to adopt.

What was said was that, if you are willing to adopt this following the problem in your community or in your state, come up and indicate. The states that first showed interest, it was conditioned to say that, if you want to train, the admission should not be competitive. The admission should be that the community should identify among their own.

Somebody who they will send for training, government will sponsor the training and, on return, be absorbed into the service. Once the person is back again, the person is bounded not to move out of that community for two years. He or she remains in the community and then, if they want to progress, at that time, they can return back to school to be a full fledged midwife or a nurse.
Now, when it was said like that, it was only one state that first responded. Okay, sorry. It was only one state that responded to that.

That was Zanfara State. Immediately after, when people saw the result coming up from Zanfara State, additional several states indicated interest. They came on board and, after that, we have done a survey to see what is happening in those states and we have gotten a good result from those states where the community midwives are presently serving.
The maternal death has reduced drastically. Now, the federal government saw it and directed that it shouldn't be an optional thing again. Every state in Nigeria should embark.
That was just done in 2024. That is where we are now with the situation. Prior to this, it was the community health extension workers that were managing the centers.

For these people that are in these localities now, these eight states now, we have gotten a drastic reduction in maternal death. They are being supported by the communities. The communities enable them, invite them to counsel the community, advise, and then they are motivated with additional allowances.
That is the present situation. Thank you. Thank you very much.

I think we've just heard from Burkina Faso, Nigeria the evidence of why women are dying and the need to respond. The examples of, as Prof said, that we have midwives already existing in our continent and we can actually make them work. We've seen from these two examples, one in terms of humanitarian situations, in security situations, they came up with proposals, ideas, and strategies to have midwives deployed and retained.

In those hard to reach in the rural areas, we've seen how even engaging the community, bonding, the midwives are from that community to get a chance to be trained but then to come back and serve. I'm sure through a rotation, we have possibility to have these areas always staffed by midwives. These are things we need to see how we can expand going forward.

As we're about to wind up, I think we're going to ask each of you to respond to one question in particular. From Africa CDC, for me, you've provided to us the evidence. We know why women are dying, but you also understand the health workforce issues within the continent.

What is your one advice in terms of what can we do in terms of strengthening midwifery programs to address these preventable maternal deaths? As you mentioned, it's hemorrhaging steps, things that we can actually prevent. What do you think us going forward can improve the midwifery program to respond to what you've seen as the causes? Also, Prof, we got great evidence from Senegal and Kenya. We've seen where midwifery can lead and we've seen when they need to be supported or collaborate with doctors.

These were two countries. What do you have to say for the others? What can they learn from this? Over to you first from CDC and then from Prof. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, for that wonderful question. We are very happy to respond to it.

If we look at the evidence, three main critical issues help us reduce maternal mortality. One of them is access to emergency obstetric and newborn care services. The second one is skilled but attendant, and the third one is family planning services.

When we did our survey, we felt the skills that you should empower to the midwives and the doctors, that in another words called the frontline managers, was very key. Then we designed a training model that answers that. Looking at the resource implications now, you can't prioritize all the 55 members at a pool.

Then we started with the 25 that recorded the highest maternal mortality. In each of these countries, we get two people trained, and eventually we got about 10 African Union member states that formed the pool of the trainers. For sustainability purpose, you need to have 10 people to train others.
We collaborated with Liverpool Tropical Medicine and we trained the first set in Kenya. The second set followed. The first set was the index training we did for all.

Then we got trainers out of them who are back now in domesticating those trainings. We were supported by the World Bank to buy the equipment for the training to the tune of $105,000. We have the training equipment.
The next point is to cascade those trainings. We have a training plan that will go into the region. We work with our regional collaborating centers.

For Africa CDC, in each of the regions, we have our offices. We are working with these offices with the member states to sustain that capacity building aspect. There are other things that maybe with time, I cannot get to.
Thank you. Professor, one advice to the other countries. We saw Senegal and Kenya.
What about the others? Thank you. That's a brilliant question because the other countries also have models of care. I'm sure they're just different.

We saw the difference between Senegal and Kenya. We have a different strategy in South Africa. All the other countries need to do a needs analysis to find out what are the innovations within this that we can teach each other from.
Unless we do our analysis, we don't know the gaps that are there. We don't know the barriers to what is existing. We don't know how to keep the midwives in Africa because that is a huge problem.

One of the things that we did in South Africa is OSD, Occupational Specific Dispensation, where midwives are well paid. They can't be well paid if also the resources that they need are not there. We need first to identify what are the types or the models that we have and how are they integrated within our health system in order for them to be highly performing.

Having started with Kenya and Senegal, we can learn lessons from the outcomes that came from there and all the other countries that are implementing. We can learn about what are the barriers and facilitators of the midwifery models of care. From the two countries, but it has to be one sentence.

We're going to see where is the full stop. One sentence. What would you recommend to governments in Nigeria to build on this success? Also from Burkina Faso, what would you recommend to government to build on the success? One sentence.
Adopt the midwifery model of care. Thank you. Okay.

Burkina Faso, how would you recommend to the government to build on the success you've just shared? What would you recommend? Thank you for the question. I think all these strategies have proven to be very effective. First of all, we have to maintain the assets.
This is very important. All these strategies are effective, so we maintain them. Secondly, we have to work to have endogenous funding.

In Burkina Faso, locally, there are many things that are being done in total resilience to be able to improve the living and working conditions of elderly women. Also, we have to avoid waste. We have to affect the resources in the positions or in the situations that need to be implemented.
In other words, we have to improve efficiency. Okay. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much for the gender balance panel. I see the ladies have protected the men by putting them in the middle. Thank you very much.
As our lovely speakers take their photo, let's hear it for one more time. Going after lunch isn't ever easy. Thank you.
Okay. Now you all get a treat, too. The tea break is set up outside.

For anyone who needs a little extra caffeine, we have you taken care of. Please go ahead, get your tea, and you're headed back to your breakout sessions. All my table facilitators, raise your hands for me.
We are doing accelerators four and five in this session. You all are doing amazing. Grab your tea, head back to your breakout, and come back to us at 1620 for our final plenary.
Thanks, everybody.
